scenarios.name: Escalation in Ukraine-Russia Conflict
scenarios.description: Renewed fighting in eastern Ukraine leads to higher energy prices, supply chain disruptions, and increased geopolitical risk, affecting US inflation, trade balance, and growth.

impacts.explanation: Higher energy costs and supply chain disruptions reduce investment and consumption, lowering GDP.
Job losses in energy-intensive sectors increase unemployment.
Higher oil prices push up CPI.
Fed likely holds rates steady amid inflation concerns.
Higher inflation expectations raise yields.
Higher borrowing to finance deficit amid lower growth.
Increased oil imports widen the deficit.
Reduced manufacturing activity due to higher input costs.
Lower consumer confidence and spending reduce retail sales.
Higher mortgage rates and lower demand slow construction.
Job cuts in sectors affected by higher energy costs.

scenarios.reasoning: Based on recent escalation in Ukraine and heightened geopolitical risk, historical data shows a 20% probability of significant energy price shocks affecting US inflation and trade, while the outside view of past conflict impacts suggests moderate likelihood; probabilistic thinking and outside view guide the 0.20 probability.

scenarios.name: US-China Trade Agreement
scenarios.description: Negotiations lead to reduced tariffs and improved market access, boosting exports, lowering inflation, and improving trade balance.

impacts.explanation: Reduced tariffs boost exports and investment, raising GDP.
Higher export demand creates jobs, lowering unemployment.
Lower import prices reduce CPI.
Fed maintains stance as inflation eases.
Improved growth outlook lowers yield expectations.
Growth increases tax revenues, offsetting debt rise.
Reduced trade deficit due to higher exports.
Stronger manufacturing demand from abroad.
Increased consumer spending from higher wages and confidence.
Lower borrowing costs and stronger demand boost construction.
Job creation in export-oriented sectors.

scenarios.reasoning: Trade tensions have eased in recent months with signs of a potential agreement, and historical trade deal success rates suggest a 15% chance; outside view and diverse sources support this probability.

Increased borrowing to fund stimulus.
No direct impact on trade balance.
Infrastructure spending boosts manufacturing.
Higher disposable income from stimulus raises retail sales.
Mortgage credit and demand increase housing starts.
Public and private sector hiring from stimulus.

scenarios.name: Global Economic Slowdown
scenarios.description: Europe and Asia experience recession, reducing external demand for US goods and services.

impacts.explanation: Weak demand from Europe and Asia reduces U.S. exports and production.
Higher unemployment due to reduced labor demand.
Lower demand reduces price pressures.
Fed may cut rates to support the economy.
Lower growth expectations lower yields.
Debt unchanged in short term.
Reduced exports worsen the trade deficit.
Lower external demand reduces manufacturing output.
Weaker consumer spending lowers retail sales.
Lower demand and financing slow construction.
Job losses in export sectors.

scenarios.reasoning: Weak demand from Europe and Asia reduces external demand, with a 15% probability of contagion affecting US growth; outside view and granular analysis guide the estimate.

scenarios.name: Federal Reserve Rate Cut
scenarios.description: Fed cuts rates by 25 basis points in response to slowing growth, lowering yields and stimulating the economy.

impacts.explanation: Lower rates stimulate borrowing and investment.
Cheaper credit encourages hiring.
Lower demand and cost pressures reduce CPI.
Fed cuts rates to support growth.
Lower yields reflect accommodative policy.
Debt unchanged in short term.
No direct impact on trade balance.
Stimulus boosts manufacturing activity.
Lower borrowing costs increase consumer spending.
Lower mortgage rates boost housing construction.
Job growth from increased demand.

scenarios.reasoning: Fed policy statements indicate a possible rate cut if data weakens, and historical rate cut frequencies suggest a 10% chance; inside view and probabilistic thinking guide the estimate.
